checks.prompt: Three requirements arrive. (a) A meeting tool must attribute each sentence of a transcript to a participant, without knowing who the participants are. (b) A building-access system must confirm a caller is the specific enrolled employee they claim to be. (c) A call centre records each side of a call on its own channel and wants per-side analytics. Which one is diarisation, and what should be done for the others?
checks.explanation: Diarisation answers who spoke when, with anonymous discovered labels — it does not say what was said and it does not say who anybody is. Confirming that a voice belongs to a specific enrolled person is verification, a different task with enrolled identities. And when each speaker already has their own channel, the structure diarisation would recover is already there: process each channel separately and skip the clustering entirely.
options: (a) is diarisation: it partitions the audio into homogeneous stretches and labels each with an ANONYMOUS tag, discovering how many speakers there are and when each talks, without identifying anybody. (b) is verification against an enrolled identity, a different task entirely. And (c) should not diarise at all — the channels are already separated, so each one is processed on its own
(b) is diarisation, because matching a voice to a person is what speaker clustering does; (a) needs recognition and (c) needs diarisation on the mixed-down audio
All three are diarisation, differing only in how many speakers are expected
(a) is diarisation and (c) is too, since separate channels still need clustering to confirm which speaker is on which channel; (b) is transcription

checks.prompt: Describe diarisation as clustering voice fingerprints along a timeline, naming the stages in order and what each contributes. Identify which stage is the crux and why. Then explain the consequence of the labels being cluster identifiers rather than names — for scoring a system, and for tracking one person across several recordings.
checks.expected: A correct answer must give the stages in order: voice activity detection to keep only speech and drop silence and noise; segmentation into short windows, ideally aware of when two people talk at once; an embedding model mapping each window to a fixed-length vector; and clustering of those vectors into groups, producing a timeline of turns with a label each. The crux must be identified as the embedding and clustering pair, and the reason given: the embedding model is trained so that the same voice lands in the same region of a vector space, which is what makes an ordinary clustering algorithm — agglomerative with a distance threshold when the count is unknown, or constrained when it is known — sufficient to recover speakers. It follows that the process is unsupervised at inference: nobody is identified, the groups are simply discovered. The consequence of arbitrary labels must be drawn twice. For scoring, a hypothesis that is perfectly correct but uses different names would look completely wrong unless an optimal correspondence between reference and hypothesis labels is found first, so the metric includes that mapping step. For tracking a person across recordings, the labels carry no meaning between files — a given tag in one file has no relationship to the same tag in another — so following an individual across recordings needs speaker identification or verification on top, not diarisation alone. Noting that modern toolkits fold all four stages into one trained pipeline while the mental model still describes what happens inside is a plus.

checks.prompt: A team reports a diarisation error rate of 10% and concludes that 90% of the words in their transcript are attributed correctly. They also compare it against a published figure of 8% from another system. What is wrong with both conclusions?
checks.explanation: The headline metric is a time-based error rate: missed speech plus falsely detected speech plus speaker confusion, divided by the total reference speech time. It is not word accuracy, and because falsely detected speech is included in the numerator it is not even bounded by one. Comparing two published figures also requires knowing how each was computed — whether a small forgiveness margin around turn boundaries was allowed and whether overlapping speech was scored — because those choices move the number a lot.
options: The metric is measured over speech TIME, not words, and it mixes three different failures — speech the system missed, speech it invented, and speech attributed to the wrong speaker — divided by the total reference speech time. So it says nothing directly about word attribution, and because invented speech is counted it can even exceed 100%. And the comparison is unsound unless both numbers were computed the same way: whether a forgiveness margin around boundaries was allowed and whether overlapping speech was scored change the figure substantially
The metric is over words, so the first conclusion is right, but the comparison is invalid because the other system used a different number of speakers
The metric is a proper accuracy bounded between zero and one, so both conclusions are sound provided the audio was the same length
The metric only counts speaker confusion, so it understates the error; the comparison is fine because the metric is standardised and admits no options

checks.prompt: Implement the evaluation and the exchange format. Write `to_frames(segments, step=0.1, end=8.0)` turning a list of `(speaker, start, stop)` tuples into a list of `int(round(end / step))` entries, each the speaker covering that frame or None, ignoring any index outside the timeline. Write `best_mapping(reference, hypothesis)` taking two such frame lists and returning the mapping from hypothesis labels to reference labels that maximises the number of frames where both are speech and the mapped label matches — searching over assignments of DISTINCT reference labels to hypothesis labels, and returning an empty dict when the hypothesis has no labels. Write `der(reference, hypothesis, step=0.1, end=8.0)` returning `{"total", "missed", "false_alarm", "confusion", "der", "mapping"}`, where `total` is the number of reference speech frames (raising `ValueError` if it is zero), `missed` counts frames where the reference has speech and the hypothesis does not, `false_alarm` the reverse, `confusion` frames where both have speech but the mapped label differs, and `der` is the three summed and divided by `total`. Write `write_rttm(segments, uri="file")` producing one line per segment of the form `SPEAKER <uri> 1 <start> <duration> <NA> <NA> <speaker> <NA> <NA>` with start and duration to three decimal places, joined by newlines. Write `parse_rttm(text)` returning the `(speaker, start, start + duration)` tuples, skipping blank lines and raising `ValueError` for a line whose first field is not `SPEAKER` or which has fewer than eight fields. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The mapping step is not a technicality, and the assertions show why: rename every cluster, or swap which cluster is which, and a perfect result still scores perfectly — without that step an entirely correct system would look like a total failure, because the labels were never meant to mean anything. Splitting the errors into three kinds is equally deliberate. Drifting boundaries produce pure confusion; a system that simply drops a stretch of speech produces misses; and a system that hears speech in silence produces false alarms — and that last case is the one that shows this is not an accuracy at all, since inventing speech pushes the score above one. The format at the end is worth noticing too: each line carries a start and a DURATION rather than an end, which is a reliable source of off-by-one-turn bugs when writing an exporter by hand.
checks.test:
REFERENCE = [("A", 0, 3), ("B", 3, 6), ("A", 6, 8)]

frames = to_frames(REFERENCE)
assert len(frames) == 80
assert frames[0] == "A" and frames[29] == "A" and frames[30] == "B"
assert frames[59] == "B" and frames[60] == "A" and frames[79] == "A"
assert to_frames([], end=1.0) == [None] * 10
assert to_frames([("A", 0, 0.5)], end=1.0).count("A") == 5
# A segment reaching past the end is clipped rather than growing the timeline.
assert len(to_frames([("A", 0, 99)], end=1.0)) == 10

# Cluster labels are arbitrary, so scoring MUST find the best correspondence first
# -- otherwise a perfect result with different names would score as a total failure.
perfect = [("spk1", 0, 3), ("spk2", 3, 6), ("spk1", 6, 8)]
result = der(REFERENCE, perfect)
assert result["der"] == 0.0, result
assert result["mapping"] == {"spk1": "A", "spk2": "B"}, result["mapping"]
# Rename every hypothesis label and nothing about the score changes.
renamed = [("zzz", 0, 3), ("aaa", 3, 6), ("zzz", 6, 8)]
assert der(REFERENCE, renamed)["der"] == 0.0
# Swap which cluster is which and it is still perfect.
swapped = [("spk2", 0, 3), ("spk1", 3, 6), ("spk2", 6, 8)]
assert der(REFERENCE, swapped)["der"] == 0.0

# Boundaries that drift produce speaker confusion, and nothing else.
drifting = [("spk1", 0, 2.7), ("spk2", 2.7, 5.5), ("spk1", 5.5, 8)]
result = der(REFERENCE, drifting)
assert result["total"] == 80, result
assert result["confusion"] == 8, result
assert result["missed"] == 0 and result["false_alarm"] == 0, result
assert abs(result["der"] - 0.10) < 1e-12, result

# The three error kinds are counted separately, because they mean different things.
missing = [("spk1", 0, 3), ("spk1", 6, 8)]
result = der(REFERENCE, missing)
assert result["missed"] == 30 and result["confusion"] == 0, result
assert abs(result["der"] - 30 / 80) < 1e-12, result

quiet_reference = [("A", 0, 2)]
noisy = [("spk1", 0, 2), ("spk2", 4, 8)]
result = der(quiet_reference, noisy)
assert result["false_alarm"] == 40, result
assert result["missed"] == 0 and result["confusion"] == 0, result
# ...which is why the score is NOT an accuracy: inventing speech can push it past 1.
assert result["der"] > 1.0, result["der"]
assert abs(result["der"] - 2.0) < 1e-12, result["der"]

# An empty hypothesis misses everything, which is a score of exactly one.
assert der(REFERENCE, [])["der"] == 1.0
assert der(REFERENCE, [])["missed"] == 80
try:
    der([], [("spk1", 0, 1)])
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a reference with no speech must be refused")

# The exchange format is one line per turn carrying start and DURATION, not an end.
rttm = write_rttm(REFERENCE, uri="meeting")
lines = rttm.splitlines()
assert len(lines) == 3, lines
fields = lines[1].split()
assert fields[0] == "SPEAKER" and fields[1] == "meeting"
assert fields[3] == "3.000" and fields[4] == "3.000", fields
assert fields[7] == "B", fields
assert parse_rttm(rttm) == [("A", 0.0, 3.0), ("B", 3.0, 6.0), ("A", 6.0, 8.0)]
assert parse_rttm(write_rttm(perfect)) == [("spk1", 0.0, 3.0), ("spk2", 3.0, 6.0),
                                           ("spk1", 6.0, 8.0)]
assert parse_rttm("") == []
for bad in ("SPEECH file 1 0.0 1.0 <NA> <NA> A <NA> <NA>", "SPEAKER file 1 0.0"):
    try:
        parse_rttm(bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad!r} must be refused")

# A round trip through the format leaves the score unchanged.
assert der(parse_rttm(write_rttm(REFERENCE)),
           parse_rttm(write_rttm(drifting)))["der"] == der(REFERENCE, drifting)["der"]

checks.prompt: A first run fails to load the pretrained pipeline with an authorisation error. Once that is resolved, results on short two-person recordings are poor — the system reports four or five speakers — and results on a stereo call recording are worse still. What are the three causes?
checks.explanation: Three first-run realities. The pipeline is gated, and the licence has to be accepted for both the pipeline and the segmentation model it depends on before a token will work — this is the most common initial failure. The speaker count is estimated by default and that estimate is unreliable on short or noisy audio, so supplying the known count or bounds is one of the largest available accuracy gains. And the models expect single-channel audio at a specific rate, so stereo at a different rate degrades results silently — though in this case the better answer is not to diarise at all, since separate channels already separate the speakers.
options: The pretrained pipeline is gated: its licence must be accepted on the model page AND on the segmentation model it depends on, with a valid access token supplied. The invented extra speakers are the pipeline estimating the count itself, which is unreliable on short or noisy audio — passing the known number, or bounds on it, is a large accuracy improvement. And the stereo recording should be resampled and downmixed to single-channel audio at the expected rate first, or, better, its channels processed separately since they already separate the speakers

The authorisation error means the token lacks write access; the extra speakers indicate overlapping speech, which cannot be fixed; and stereo input is handled automatically so its poor result must be a codec problem
All three come from running on a processor without an accelerator, which disables the segmentation model and forces a fallback clusterer
The authorisation error is transient; the extra speakers mean the distance threshold is too low and should be removed entirely; and stereo should be summed to mono only after diarisation

checks.prompt: Compare this toolkit with a combined transcription-and-diarisation pipeline, with a vendor speech framework's own diarisation, with a managed cloud service, and with simply processing separate channels. Say when each wins. Then advise a hospital transcribing consultations recorded on a single microphone, where the recordings must stay on their own hardware and the transcript must attribute each sentence to either the clinician or the patient. Say what you would use and what specific setting you would supply.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all five. This toolkit wins when you want open, on-premises diarisation with full control and good accuracy, at the cost of gated models, a heavy framework dependency and tuning. The combined pipeline wins when you want a transcript AND speaker labels in one step, though it wraps this same toolkit underneath, inheriting the same gating while giving less control. The vendor framework's own diarisation wins for teams already inside that ecosystem with the hardware to match, at the cost of a heavier setup. A managed cloud service wins when diarisation as an API flag with no operational burden is acceptable, at the cost of per-minute charges, audio leaving the premises and less tunability. Processing separate channels wins outright when the recording already has one speaker per channel — then diarisation is unnecessary. The recommendation must respect the stated constraint that recordings stay on the hospital's own hardware, which rules out the managed service; a single microphone rules out the per-channel shortcut; and since a transcript with attribution is wanted, either the combined pipeline or this toolkit alongside a transcription model is appropriate, with the words joined to the turns by time. The specific setting must be named: the number of speakers is known to be two, so supplying that — rather than letting the pipeline estimate it — is the single largest accuracy improvement available, particularly on short consultations. A strong answer notes that the labels are anonymous, so deciding which cluster is the clinician requires something outside diarisation, and that overlapping speech and very short back-channel utterances remain the hardest cases and should be measured on real recordings rather than assumed.
